Seminar Title:

Study of neutrinoless double beta decay and anomalous magnetic moment of Muon in left-right symmetric models

Seminar Type:

Abstract:

The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics, despite its remarkable success, fails to address several fundamental issues, such as the origin of neutrino masses and the flavor puzzle, thereby necessitating physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM). Among various extensions, the Left-right symmetric models (LRSM) provide an elegant framework that restores parity symmetry at high energies and naturally explains light neutrino masses through type-I and type-II seesaw mechanisms. Since these scales lie beyond the reach of current colliders, precision low-energy observables serve as crucial indirect probes of new physics. This work focuses on two such observables, (a) neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$) and (b) Muon anomalous magnetic moment&nbsp $(g-2)_\mu$, within the LRSM framework. We explore how the interplay of seesaw dominances influences these processes across three neutrino generations. In particular, the unconventional neutrino-gamma-neutrino vertex yields a contribution to $(g-2)_\mu$ nearly seven orders of magnitude larger than the Standard Model expectation, potentially accounting for the observed discrepancy. The analysis identifies the type-II dominated seesaw configuration as the most stable and phenomenologically viable scenario. Furthermore, the study extends to the supersymmetric left-right model (SUSYLRM), which not only addresses the hierarchy problem but also introduces natural candidates for dark matter. Within this setup, $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay is analyzed using effective operator methods, revealing that the lightest sneutrino and neutralino can simultaneously mediate the decay and act as viable candidates for dark matter. Overall, this work demonstrates how low-energy precision observables can effectively bridge collider-scale and cosmological phenomena, offering a unified window into high-scale symmetries and interactions.
